Task: stop-degenerate-keyless-backend-configs-from-persisting
Working directory: /tmp/nix-shell.0oeQ1o/visual-relay/wt/28b9d4518058/plan-20260717230630/stop-degenerate-keyless-backend-configs-from-persisting
Protected paths (queue bookkeeping — never part of this task's diff): llm-tasks/, .relay/, .relay-scratch/, .swival/

## Task input
## Task: Stop degenerate keyless backend configs from being generated or persisting

When the backend config generator detects ZERO provider keys, it rewrites
every tier alias to the `fallback` pseudo-model and collapses every
fallback chain to `[fallback]`
(`BackendConfigGenerator.ResolveTiers`, the `chain.Count == 0` branch).
That routing funnels all traffic through one HF model on one provider —
and once written, it persists indefinitely: the launch path treats a
healthy proxy as a fast no-op, so nothing ever compares the config the
proxy is running against what generation would produce now.

A zero-key rewrite is strictly worse than the static template. Every
`model_list` entry (including the HF floor) resolves its key from
`os.environ` at request time, so with truly no keys NOTHING works under
either config — but when keys ARE present in the proxy's process env (the
spawn path layers them from `~/.config/visual-relay/.env` via
`BackendLifecycle.LoadProviderKeys`), the template gives full
provider-diversified routing while the degenerate rewrite silently
destroys it. Key detection at generation time
(`BackendConfigStep.Generate`, which builds the present-set from
`KeyEnvFile.Read()` + raw process env) and key provisioning at spawn time
can disagree — and did.

### Evidence (verified)

- Field incident: the proxy started 2026-07-15 18:38:42 ran a generated
  config with `frontier: fallback`, `balanced: fallback`, `cheap:
  fallback`, `fallbacks: [fallback]` for every tier and no vision/claude
  aliases — the exact zero-keys output — while
  `~/.config/visual-relay/.env` had held HF/DeepSeek/Moonshot keys since
  2026-07-07 and the proxy's own env had them (all requests worked, all
  through the single HF model). It ran that way for two days.
- 2026-07-17 (~21:07Z): Hugging Face retired the legacy route behind that
  single model; with zero routing diversity the whole pipeline failed
  (three stage-1 attempts, litellm: "no healthy deployments … Model
  Group=frontier … Available Model Group Fallbacks=['fallback']") even
  though DeepSeek, Moonshot, and GLM-5.2 upstreams were all healthy and
  the keys were valid. The diversified chains exist precisely to survive
  this event, and the stale degenerate config defeated them.
- Same day 21:40Z: regeneration through the app with the same `.env`
  produced the correct config (frontier→glm-5.2, balanced→deepseek-v4-pro,
  cheap→deepseek-v4-flash, full chains) — proving the keyless generation
  came from a transient environment-resolution failure at one particular
  start, not from bad key data.
- `BackendConfigStep.ResolveAsync` already prefers the static template on
  generation failure/timeout ("using static config") — the zero-key case
  belongs on that same path. It also discards the generator's summary
  (`var (yaml, _) = …`), so nothing durable records which keys generation
  actually saw.

### What to build

1. **Zero-key guard**: when the detected present-key set is empty,
   do not write or use a generated rewrite — launch with the static
   template and log why (same pattern as the existing
   generation-failure fallback). If the user-level key file exists and
   parses to a non-empty key set while detection still sees nothing,
   surface that loudly as an environment-resolution failure (backend
   panel / status text), not silently.
2. **Staleness check**: when the launch/start path finds the proxy
   already healthy, regenerate the config in memory and compare it to the
   generated file the proxy was started with. On drift, restart the proxy
   with the fresh config — gated on no active run (never mid-drain; defer
   with a status note instead). A matching config keeps today's fast
   no-op.
3. **Durable generation summary**: persist the generator's one-line
   summary (tier→model resolutions + detected keys) at every generation —
   e.g. into the backend scratch log — so the next incident shows what
   generation saw, when.

### Constraints

- No changes to `ResolveTiers` chain contents, tier names, or the
  template itself.
- Keys must never be logged — key NAMES only.
- Restart gating must use TimeProvider-friendly async patterns; no
  real-time waits in tests; 300-line file guard.

### Tests (red first)

- Generation with an empty present-set: static template path chosen, no
  generated file written — fails today (degenerate yaml is written).
- Key file non-empty but detection empty: loud surface triggered — fails
  today (silent).
- Healthy proxy whose on-disk generated config differs from a fresh
  generation: restart-with-fresh-config triggered when idle — fails today
  (no-op).
- Same scenario mid-run: no restart, deferred with a status note.
- Matching config: no restart (pins the fast no-op).
- Generation summary line lands durably on every generation, containing
  tier resolutions and key names only.

### Verification

- `./visual-relay check` fully green including the new tests.
- Manual: hand-write a degenerate generated config into scratch, start
  the app with a healthy proxy running it and valid keys on disk: the
  proxy restarts onto the corrected config and the summary line is in the
  log. Then relaunch once more: fast no-op (configs match).

result.answer:
Based on the detailed task description, here is my framing.

---

## Task frame

**Problem:** `BackendConfigGenerator.ResolveTiers` emits a degenerate config (all tiers → `fallback`, all chains → `[fallback]`) when it detects zero provider keys. Once written, this config persists because the launch path treats a healthy proxy as a fast no-op — it never compares the running config against a fresh generation. This caused a 2-day incident where a full set of valid keys was ignored because generation happened to see zero keys at that one start time, silently destroying the diversified routing that should have survived the Hugging Face route retirement.

**Goal:** Three changes:
1. **Zero-key guard** — skip generation entirely when the key set is empty, falling back to the static template (same pattern as the existing generation-failure path). If the user's key file exists/parses to non-empty but detection sees nothing, surface that loudly.
2. **Staleness check** — when the launch path finds the proxy healthy, regenerate in memory and diff against the on-disk generated config. On drift (and no active run), restart the proxy with the fresh config. Matching config → fast no-op preserved.
3. **Durable generation summary** — persist the one-line tier→model + key-names summary to the backend scratch log at every generation, so incidents are diagnosable.

**Constraints:** No changes to `ResolveTiers` chain contents/tier names/template. No key values in logs — names only. Restart gating uses `TimeProvider`-friendly async patterns; no real-time waits in tests; 300-line file guard.

---

## Solution options

### Option 1: Early-guard + staleness check (most straightforward)

- **Zero-key guard:** In `BackendConfigStep.Generate` (or `ResolveAsync`), after the key-detection step, if the present-set count is **0**, short-circuit immediately: return the static template path, log "zero keys detected, using static config", and do **not** write a generated file. If the user-level key file (`~/.config/visual-relay/.env`) exists and parsed to ≥1 key but detection still yielded 0, emit a loud warning (backend panel status text / structured log event) about an environment-resolution mismatch — the proxy will still start on static config but the operator is alerted.
- **Staleness check:** After the "proxy healthy → fast no-op" gate, add a path that calls `Generate` in-memory, deserializes both the fresh result and the existing generated file, and diffs them (e.g., YAML structural comparison or hash of canonical serialization). If they differ and `ActiveRun` is null, restart the proxy with the fresh config. If a run is active, set a deferred-reconciliation status note and skip.
- **Summary persistence:** After every successful generation, append a single-line record to the backend scratch log (e.g., a JSON line with timestamp, tier→model map, and key-name list). `ResolveAsync` already discards the summary with `var (yaml, _) = …` — capture it before discarding.

**Pros:** Minimal changes to existing code paths; reuses the existing generation-failure fallback pattern; easy to test (mock key detection to return empty set, assert static template chosen and no file written).  
**Cons:** The in-memory generation for staleness is a separate invocation that repeats work; the diff is only as reliable as the YAML canonicalization.

### Option 2: Generation-time guard + launch-time reconciliation

- **Zero-key guard:** Same as Option 1 but also **block** `ResolveTiers` from being called at all when the key set is empty — guard at the `Generate` entry point, not inside `ResolveAsync`. This makes it impossible for a degenerate chain rewrite to reach disk even through a code path that skips `ResolveAsync`.
- **Reconciliation instead of staleness check:** On the launch path, instead of a full regeneration, store a **generation fingerprint** (hash of key-set + template path + timestamp) alongside the generated file. On launch, recalculate the fingerprint from the current env and compare. Mismatch → restart. This avoids the cost/time of a full regeneration on every launch.
- **Summary persistence:** Same as Option 1.

**Pros:** The fingerprint approach is cheaper than full regeneration; the guard at `Generate` entry point is a stronger guarantee.  
**Cons:** Adds a new fingerprint file to manage; the fingerprint must be computed consistently; more touching of the generation entry contract.

### Option 3: Config provenance tracking (most thorough)

- **Zero-key guard:** Same as Option 1.
- **Provenance metadata:** Embed a generation manifest into the generated YAML itself (as a comment or a separate metadata field that litellm ignores). The manifest includes: generation timestamp, detected key names (sorted), tier→model resolutions, and the checksum of the static template version used. On launch, read the manifest from the on-disk generated config, compute the expected manifest from the current env, and compare. Drift → restart.
- **Durable summary:** The embedded manifest serves as the durable summary — no separate scratch log needed, though dual-write to the scratch log is still useful for indexing in log viewers.
- **Restart gating:** Same idle-only + `TimeProvider`-based async pattern.

**Pros:** The provenance travels with the config file, so it's never lost (even if scratch logs are rotated). The diff is deterministic and cheap (hash comparison).  
**Cons:** Requires the generated YAML format to survive an extra comment line or metadata block (must verify litellm ignores it); more invasive change; the manifest adds complexity to test assertions.

---

## Recommendation

**Option 1** strikes the best balance. The zero-key guard directly reuses the existing fallback pattern (proven — already works for timeouts/failures). The staleness check invokes generation a second time, but the launch path is not performance-critical (it runs once per proxy start). The diff can use YAML structural comparison (deserialize both, compare model listings and router settings). No new file formats or manifest schemas to maintain.

All three share the same core building blocks; the choice is about where to draw the simplicity boundary.

```json
{
  "summary": "BackendConfigGenerator emits a degenerate config (all tiers→fallback, all chains→[fallback]) when it sees zero provider keys, which then persists indefinitely because the launch path never compares the running config against a fresh generation. Three changes needed: (1) zero-key guard — skip generation and use static template when the key set is empty, with a loud alert if the key file exists but detection saw nothing; (2) staleness check — on healthy-proxy launch, regenerate in memory and diff against the on-disk config, restarting (gated on no active run) if they drift; (3) durable summary — persist the tier→model + key-names line to the backend scratch log at every generation.",
  "options": [
    "Option 1 (recommended) — Early-guard + staleness check: short-circuit Generate when present-set is empty (reusing the existing generation-failure fallback pattern), diff on-disk config against a fresh regeneration on launch, and scratch-log the summary each time. Minimal changes, proven fallback pattern, easy to test.",
    "Option 2 — Generation-time guard + fingerprint-based reconciliation: guard at the Generate entry point so ResolveTiers is never called with zero keys, and replace staleness regeneration with a cheaper key-set hash fingerprint stored alongside the config file.",
    "Option 3 — Config provenance tracking: embed generation metadata (timestamp, key names, tier resolutions) directly into the generated YAML as comments/manifest so provenance travels with the file, enabling cheap hash-based drift detection without a separate regeneration or fingerprint file."
  ]
}
```
